Article Title: 'Only openers' spots are permanent': Gautam Gambhir's clear message on India's T20 batting order
Article Text:
Abhishek Sharma and Sanju Samson (Image credit: Agencies)

'Only the openers are permanent'

Samson's 82 goes in vain as West Indies script record chase

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India head coach Gautam Gambhir has backed the decision to promote Shivam Dube to No. 4 despite the all-rounder failing to make an impact in the second T20 International against the West Indies in Ranchi.Dube scored seven off 10 balls before being dismissed by West Indies off-spinner Roston Chase. However, Gambhir said India would continue to change their batting order according to the match situation, adding that only the opening positions are fixed in T20 cricket.Dube was promoted to No. 4 after Ishan Kishan 's dismissal, with Shreyas Iyer coming in later. India backed Dube to take on the spin bowling despite Chase's success against left-handed batters."We have used him like this for a long time, including during the World Cup and before it. It is not as though this was a one-off decision today," Gambhir said at the post-match media interaction at the JSCA Stadium.India lost momentum in the middle overs after losing wickets in successive overs, including top-scorer Sanju Samson . Iyer and Tilak Varma, however, scored quick runs towards the end to take India to 249/5.Gambhir stood by the decision to send Dube in at No. 4 and said the team would continue to be flexible with its batting order."This is international cricket. Sometimes things go your way, and sometimes they don't."We lost momentum today, but we have also gained a lot of momentum by sending him in at No. 4, where he has taken on the opposition bowlers," the coach said."More importantly, I think we have always been flexible with our batting order, and we will continue to do that. I have always said since taking over that in T20 cricket, only the openers are permanent. The rest of the batting order should remain flexible.”India's total of 249/5 was not enough as the West Indies chased down the target in just 18.3 overs to level the five-match series 1-1. Samson led India's batting with 82, while Iyer scored 40 off 18 balls and Tilak remained unbeaten on 44 off 18 deliveries.Samson and Kishan added 97 runs for the second wicket. Samson reached his half-century in just 21 balls, while Kishan scored 43 off 22 deliveries before being dismissed by Chase. The off-spinner also removed Dube for seven. Samson's innings ended in the 15th over, but Iyer and Tilak provided late runs to help India post their highest-ever T20I total against the West Indies.West Indies had a difficult start to the chase, with Mayank Yadav taking two wickets in the opening over. However, captain Shai Hope and Sherfane Rutherford turned the match around with aggressive batting against India's spinners.Hope scored an unbeaten 102 off 45 balls, hitting six fours and nine sixes. Rutherford made 84 off 37 balls, with seven fours and seven sixes. The pair added 120 runs off just 54 balls to put the West Indies in control. Mayank dropped Rutherford, and the missed chance proved costly for India.Romario Shepherd then scored 34 off 13 balls to help the visitors finish the chase in 18.3 overs and level the series 1-1.
Article Summary: India coach Gautam Gambhir backs decision to promote Shivam Dube to No. 4. Dube scored seven off 10 balls before being dismissed by West Indies off-spinner Roston Chase. India lost momentum in middle overs after losing wickets in successive overs. Shreyas Iyer and Tilak Varma scored quick runs towards the end to take India to 249/5.

Article Title: From schoolboy to biggest SA20 auction signing: How Jason Rowles became Joburg’s big bet
Article Text:
Jason Rowles, 18, became the most expensive signing at the SA20 Season 5 Auction after Joburg Super Kings secured his services for R2.9 million. (Special Arrangement)

From the Schools SA20 Finals to a R2.9 million deal, Jason Rowles has emerged as one of South Africa's most promising young cricketing talents. (Special Arrangement)

The work is being done on recognising talent, the scouting behind the scenes. I think the mindset to promote youth is important. Graeme Smith | SA20 League Commissioner

South Africa's leading run-scorer at the Under-19 World Cup, Jason Rowles is now set for a new challenge with Joburg Super Kings in SA20. (Special Arrangement)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Joburg Super Kings head coach Albie Morkel believes Jason Rowles has the talent to develop into a top player after the 18-year-old's big-money signing.(Special Arrangement)

NEW DELHI: Jason Rowles entered the SA20 Auction, ahead of the fifth season of South Africa's premier T20 competition, at a base price of R200,000 (approx. Rs 11.62 lakh). As MI Cape Town (MICT) raised the paddle, the bidding began. Joburg Super Kings (JSK) joined the bidding battle almost immediately, upping the bid by R25,000 (approx. Rs 1.47 lakh). With Durban's Super Giants and Paarl Royals not involved in the auction, the remaining teams, Pretoria Capitals and Sunrisers Eastern Cape, kept their paddles down. The bids, however, continued to rise.MICT took it to R500,000 and then to R1 million. JSK stayed in it and took it to R1.5 million. MICT upped it to R2 million. JSK took it to R2.5 million and finally outbid their rivals at R2.9 million (Rs 1.69 crore). The 18-year-old from Johannesburg, still a matric pupil at St David’s Marist Inanda, was acquired at 14.5 times his base price."Robbie [Robin Peterson, the MICT] and his crew saw the same talent that we saw in Jason. He is a local boy from Joburg that we've tracked for a long time. We had a talent scout camp a year ago, which he attended. So he was someone on our radar," said Albie Morkel , head coach of JSK, in an interaction facilitated by the SA20 after the Season 5 Auction."Did I think he was going to go for that amount of money? No, definitely not. But he's someone that we really wanted. I think in that Rookie and now the U-23 spot, every franchise is looking for that guy who's going to be the next Lhuan-dre (Pretorius) or the next (Dewald) Brevis. Whether he will be that, time will tell. But he's a really talented guy.""He's got a very good management team around him. So I'm sure, as a cricketer, with this money tag around his head now, over his head, they will manage it well. And from our side, from a coaching point of view and a franchise point of view, we'll give him every opportunity to grow into the player that we hope he will develop into," he continued.Over a year ago, however, he was playing in the Schools SA20 Finals, a T20 competition created by the SA20 and Cricket South Africa (CSA) in 2024 to spot and encourage young talent. Representing St David's Marist, Rowles's team finished runners-up in Volume 1 before he captained his school in Volume 2 last year.Rowles, a left-hand batter who can also bowl left-arm spin, has shown plenty of potential in South African cricket since. He was South Africa's leading run-scorer in the Under-19 World Cup earlier this year, scoring 280 runs in five innings at an average of 70 and a strike rate of 112. Rowles scored 98 off 93 against Afghanistan before slamming an unbeaten 125 off 101 deliveries against Tanzania.In July, he showed promise in the longer format, scoring a double hundred in the second Youth Test against England U19. This came after he scored 42, 15 and 85 in the three Youth ODIs and twin fifties in the first Youth Test.Even though 42-year-old Faf du Plessis earned as much as Rowles (R2.7 million) at the 2026 SA20 mini-auction, the flavour around the T20 franchise world is centred on youngsters. Take 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, last IPL season's Orange Cap winner, as a perfect example."The work is being done on recognising talent, the scouting behind the scenes. I think the mindset to promote youth is important. And obviously, you're talking about Sooryavanshi in the IPL. There are a number of U-23s, young players involved in our tournament. To think that Dewald Brevis is still U-23. And then you've got Jason Rowles fetching the highest number at the auction. I think for us, we are trying to grow the game of cricket. Those little stories really are nuggets in terms of helping build the kind of future talent and keeping cricket as a high-profile sport in our country that people want to be a part of," said SA20 League Commissioner Graeme Smith Spotting youth, nurturing it and investing in it is a double-edged sword. How much exposure is too much exposure? How do you ensure their talent remains untouched amid the external noise of hype, expectations and big money? It is something Indian cricket is grappling with when it comes to Sooryavanshi. Now, with Rowles entering that conversation, albeit at 18, Graeme Smith feels the players deserve the big bucks for their talent while also receiving support if needed."If you look at the world of sports, young sports talent is being paid very well across the board. Cricket is playing catch-up now with private ownership in terms of investment in youth and the increased professionalism of the game. So I think those stories are great," said former South Africa skipper Smith."Obviously, from a management perspective, we have the Players' Association in South Africa, which has a really good system in place in terms of supporting players, guiding them on financial investment and giving them support around the sport to help guide them. But if you're good enough in the world, you deserve to do well. And credit to the young talent right now that's being recognised and supported," he continued.A year after Brevis, then 22, became the most expensive signing in SA20 history (R16.5 million) and delivered on that promise for Pretoria Capitals, scoring 370 runs at an average of 41.11 and a strike rate of 156.12 to emerge as the second-highest run-scorer in Season 4, it remains to be seen how 18-year-old Rowles fares for his local franchise.
Article Summary: South Africa's leading run-scorer at the Under-19 World Cup, Jason Rowles is now set for a new challenge with Joburg Super Kings in SA20. The 18-year-old from Johannesburg, still a matric pupil at St David’s Marist Inanda, was acquired at 14.5 times his base price.

Article Title: 'I don't blame anyone': Gautam Gambhir's strong words after India fail to defend 249 vs West Indies
Article Text:
West Indies chased down a target of 250 in just 18.3 overs to register their highest successful T20I chase vs India (Image credit: Agencies)

'I don't blame anyone'

'You don't shrug off any defeat'

Mayank's early strikes not enough

Gambhir wants a fair contest between bat and ball

Hope, Rutherford power West Indies to record chase

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India head coach Gautam Gambhir refused to blame the toss, the dew or a dropped catch after India suffered a six-wicket defeat against the West Indies in the second T20I in Ranchi on Friday. Instead, he said India had to take responsibility for failing to defend a total of 249.West Indies chased down a target of 250 in just 18.3 overs to register their highest successful T20I chase against India and level the five-match series 1-1. Shai Hope scored an unbeaten 102, while Sherfane Rutherford made 84 to lead the visitors to victory.The toss proved important as heavy dew made it difficult for India's bowlers to grip the ball. Mayank Yadav also dropped Rutherford when the batter was on 38, giving him another chance to build his innings.However, Gambhir refused to blame either the conditions or the missed catch for India's defeat. He said the team had to accept that it had failed to defend a big total."I don't blame anyone, and I don't blame anything. The bottom line is that we could not defend 250. They batted extremely well, and they deserved to win."We still have a lot of work to do because, when you play against dangerous teams like the West Indies, you need to figure out how to defend a total, especially when you lose the toss," he said."The toss is not in your hands, and catches get dropped in sport. That's fine."Gambhir said India could not ignore the defeat or use the difficult bowling conditions as an excuse. He stressed that the team needed to find ways to stop opponents from chasing big totals, even on flat pitches with dew."You don't shrug off any defeat. If you want to keep improving, you don't want to sweep anything under the carpet. We are a world champion team, so we want to keep improving."Obviously, these are tough conditions to bowl in. We know that bowling on flat wickets with dew is difficult, but we need to figure out a way to stop the opposition, especially when they have lost two wickets in the first over and then three in the first six overs," he said."Obviously, it was tough, but credit to the West Indies for the way Shai Hope (102 not out) and Sherfane Rutherford (84) batted. We know they are world class batters, especially in this format. It was tough for us, but we are going to keep improving."One of India's positives was Mayank's opening spell. The fast bowler regularly clocked speeds above 140 kmph and dismissed Kamil Pooran and Shimron Hetmyer off successive deliveries in the first over. He later bowled Rovman Powell with a delivery clocked at 149 kmph.However, Gambhir said the match could not be judged by what happened in the opening over."I have played enough cricket to know that games are not decided in the first over. Obviously, the West Indies are a strong T20 side. We respect them, and we know how dangerous they are."Games are not won or lost in the first over. A game of cricket is won or lost by the way you play consistently over the course of 40 overs."Gambhir also backed Mayank to continue bowling at his natural pace."A fast bowler should bowl like a fast bowler. He is not a slower bowler."If you can bowl at 150 kmph, bowl at 150. If you can bowl at 120, bowl at 120. When you are playing as a fast bowler, it is your duty to bowl fast, like a fast bowler," he said."That is what he did today, and that is why he was successful."Asked whether India wanted better pitches after another high-scoring match, Gambhir said he wanted a good contest between bat and ball. He had earlier described the Guwahati surface as a featherbed."Don't you want a good competition between the bat and the ball? Of course, we want what you want."If you want to see sixes and fours, we want to see that as well. If you want an even contest between bat and ball, we want that too."The bowlers are our bowlers. They are not foreign bowlers. Their careers are at stake as well. They have worked hard, just like everyone else in the dressing room. If there is an even contest between bat and ball, it will be good. We will get to see better cricket.”India's inability to defend 249 came after Sanju Samson returned to form with a brilliant 82. Shreyas Iyer scored 40 off 18 balls, while Tilak Varma remained unbeaten on 44 off 18 deliveries to take India to 249/5.Samson and Ishan Kishan put on 97 runs for the second wicket. Samson reached his fifty off just 21 balls, helping India make a strong start after being asked to bat.Kishan scored 43 off 22 balls before Roston Chase dismissed him. Chase also removed Shivam Dube, who made seven, as India lost wickets in the middle overs.Samson's innings ended at 82 when he was caught in the 15th over. Iyer and Tilak then added quick runs to help India post their highest-ever T20I total against the West Indies.The visitors made a shaky start when Mayank struck twice in the opening over. But Hope and Rutherford took control of the chase, attacking India's spinners despite the difficult conditions.Hope reached his half-century off 24 balls and finished unbeaten on 102 off 45 deliveries, hitting six fours and nine sixes. Rutherford scored 84 off 37 balls, with seven fours and seven sixes.The pair added 120 runs off just 54 balls to put the West Indies firmly on course. Rutherford's dropped catch by Mayank proved costly, but Gambhir refused to use the missed chance as an excuse.Romario Shepherd then scored 34 off 13 balls to provide the final push, as the West Indies completed the chase in 18.3 overs and levelled the series 1-1.
Article Summary: West Indies chased down a target of 250 in just 18.3 overs to register their highest successful T20I chase against India. Shai Hope scored an unbeaten 102, while Sherfane Rutherford made 84 to lead the visitors to victory. Mayank Yadav also dropped Rutherford when the batter was on 38, giving him another chance to build his innings.

Article Title: BCCI Centre of Excellence treated 32 top cricketers last year
Article Text:
harshit rana, hardik pandya, jasprit bumrah

No SSM head, lack of coordination with Team India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Fifteen budgeted camps didn’t happen

Thirty-seven top men’s players opted for ‘training block’ programme

Poll Vote & Share your view Which aspect of player management do you think needs urgent improvement? Better workload management Improved coordination between medical teams 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

New Delhi: The Indian cricket board’s ( BCCI ) injury management programme at its Centre of Excellence (CoE) has been under renewed focus over the past 20 months. Now, according to the CoE annual report, accessed by TOI, as many as 32 top men’s team players, including 20 BCCI centrally contracted players and 12 players under a new targeted/India ‘A’ category, underwent rehabilitation for injuries between April 2025 and March 2026. The list has swelled post IPL 2026, with at least two players breaking down in each series.Interestingly, the report states that the BCCI increased the CoE’s budget by nearly Rs 35 crore compared to the actual expenses in the previous financial year. The CoE’s expenses include administrative costs, courses and match expenses.The CoE’s projected expenses for 2026-27 now stand at Rs 127 crore, compared to Rs 92 crore in actual expenses last year.India’s Test and ODI captain Shubman Gill and head coach Gautam Gambhir have been vocal about how difficult it has become to plan tours because of a surge in injuries over the last year. While the report does not specify how many times each player reported to the CoE, it mentions that injuries to 68 players across genders were treated and managed by the BCCI-CoE Sports Science Medicine (SSM) team.When it comes to the nature of the injuries, the majority were soft-tissue injuries.The only impact injury treatment mentioned was that of Rishabh Pant, who underwent treatment following a foot fracture sustained during a Test in Manchester in July 2025.Interestingly, the report also reveals that Rohit Sharma underwent rehabilitation at the CoE during this period, but the BCCI never made an official statement about it. Rohit last reported to the CoE for a hamstring injury following this year’s IPL.The latest Team India players added to the list up to Sept 30 this year are Virat Kohli, Varun Chakravarthy, Prince Yadav and Harsh Dubey, besides multiple ‘targeted’ players. From that list, Jasprit Bumrah, Washington Sundar, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Harshit Rana, Hardik Pandya and Prasidh Krishna have been repeat cases. Rana, Pandya and Reddy have each spent at least four months at the CoE in the last 18 months.The BCCI advertised the post of SSM head at the CoE only last month. The post has been lying vacant since Nitin Patel resigned in March 2025.TOI understands that there has been a breakdown in communication between Team India’s SSM team and the CoE’s SSM team, with cricket head VVS Laxman being the only medium of communication. It has been learnt that Team India strength and conditioning (S&C) coach Adrian Le Roux suggested a few tweaks to workload management routines in June 2025, while the CoE has been reluctant to deviate from its own mechanisms.Personnel from the CoE’s SSM team travelled to domestic tournaments to monitor key India players under the injury prevention and management programme.The last time Indian cricket saw a spate of soft-tissue injuries was in 2021-22, when players suddenly moved out of playing in bubbles during the Covid-19 pandemic. That time, the issue was brought under control in two to three months. In 2017, too, there was a three-month phase when multiple players broke down after S&C coach Shanker Basu introduced drastic changes to the fitness programme.According to the report, 15 of the 57 budgeted camps and tournaments were not conducted in the last audited year.The CoE conducted 25 elite/high-performance camps across age groups and genders, besides special camps for the north-eastern states. It also organised multiple courses and camps for S&C coaches, other coaches and match officials.The CoE started a programme called the ‘training block’ for contracted and targeted/India ‘A’ players. According to the report, 37 players, including 11 contracted players and 26 India ‘A’/targeted players, availed themselves of the programme, which focuses on strength and skill training.
Article Summary: As many as 32 top men’s team players, including 20 BCCI centrally contracted players and 12 players under a new targeted/India ‘A’ category, underwent rehabilitation for injuries between April 2025 and March 2026. The list has swelled post IPL 2026, with at least two players breaking down in each series.

Article Title: India rivals, Indian roots: The stories of Australia ‘A’ stars Nikhil Chaudhary and Tanveer Sangha
Article Text:
Nikhil Chaudhary and Tanveer Sangha (Agency Image)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Puducherry: India are Australia’s biggest on-field rivals. But these days, the Aussies are banking heavily on Indian-origin players who are making a mark at the highest level. As Australia ‘A’ continue their tour of India, two Indian-origin players brought up in different environments, Nikhil Chaudhary and Tanveer Sangha, offer fascinating stories of migration, identity, perseverance and ambition.For Nikhil, Australia was never part of the original plan. Born in Delhi and raised in Ludhiana, he was playing domestic cricket for Punjab when a holiday to Queensland during Covid-19 turned into a life-changing detour.“I was already playing for Punjab. But then I had to make that decision of going away from the family and starting a new journey,” Nikhil told TOI on the eve of Australia’s second ‘A’ one-dayer.The transition meant starting from scratch. He worked at a Mexican restaurant and drove as a courier to pay his bills before cricket began opening doors. The medium-pacer from Punjab eventually reinvented himself as a leg-spinning all-rounder and earned an Australia debut this year.“It’s just a different culture we have in India, where we just take everything for granted because of our mom and dad working hard for us. Here, I had to start from zero. If you are not hard-working and not able to struggle, then it’s not possible to actually play for Australia,” the hard-hitting middle-order batter said.His family in Ludhiana has remained his biggest support system, even though his father’s allegiance during an India-Australia contest remains firmly with the Men in Blue.“My dad still supports India. Just because I moved to Australia doesn’t mean he’s going to support Australia,” Nikhil said.Tanveer, on the other hand, never planned to become a cricketer. Born in Australia to Punjabi parents, he treated cricket as “a little more than a summer pastime”. Leg-spin entered his life around the age of 13 and, slowly, taking wickets began turning a hobby into a possible career.His parents’ journey, however, gave him a deeper appreciation of what it took to reach this level. His father, Joga, who played kabaddi in India and later in Australia, and his mother, Upneet, built their lives as migrants.“They’ve made huge sacrifices to get us here,” Tanveer said. “They’ve given me everything, the resources, their time, taking me everywhere to training and games.”Tanveer is also eyeing a return to the Australian side, with Adam Zampa currently firmly established as the first-choice leg-spinner. The youngster, however, sees Zampa’s presence as motivation rather than a roadblock.“My job is to keep getting better and hopefully take over his spot when he retires,” he said.
Article Summary: Nikhil Chaudhary and Tanveer Sangha offer fascinating stories of migration, identity, perseverance and ambition. For Nikhil, Australia was never part of the original plan. The medium-pacer from Punjab reinvented himself as a leg-spinning all-rounder and earned an Australia debut this year.Tanveer is also eyeing a return to the Australian side.

Article Title: ‘I just like to be the first in everything’: Pranavi Urs sets sights on Olympic medal
Article Text:
Gold medallist India's Pranavi Urs (REUTERS)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bengaluru: Pranavi Urs has always seemed to have a liking for firsts. In 2025, the Mysuru pro became the first Indian woman to win an open-field professional tournament against male golfers when she triumphed at the IGPL Invitational in Mumbai. Last week in Japan, she added the biggest first of them all, becoming the first Indian woman to win an individual gold at the Asian Games.“I just like to be the first in everything,” Pranavi said during an interaction facilitated by SAI. “I find ways to put myself in situations where no one’s ever been before.” For someone who has repeatedly ventured into uncharted territory, the Asian Games gold was another opportunity to test herself.The three-shot lead she carried into the final round disappeared after a triple bogey on the third hole. But unlike three years ago in Hangzhou, Pranavi knew what it was like to be in a high-pressure situation. More importantly, she had prepared for it.The night before the final round, Pranavi and her psychologist had visualised different scenarios, including what could happen if things went wrong. When the triple bogey arrived, she recognised the situation and reminded herself that she had reached rock bottom.“I was like, you’ve got nothing to lose, you’re at rock bottom now. The worst thing has already happened, so it can’t get worse,” she said.That preparation allowed her to return to the process rather than focus on the outcome. Even on the final hole, when the gold was within touching distance, she was thinking about making sure she secured a medal rather than winning it.She changed from a six-iron to a seven-iron for her second shot after feeling the adrenaline rush. She was so locked into the moment that she did not even realise her final putt was for gold.“I thought it was like, make par and maybe force a playoff,” she said. “Little did I know that the last putt that I hit was putt to win.”Hence, there was no elaborate celebration. She did not know she had won. Now, however, the significance of the gold is beginning to sink in, as is the possibility of what it could lead to.Pranavi’s next first could come on the Ladies European Tour, where she has been knocking on the door of a maiden victory. She believes her game is ready and that it is now a matter of patience.“I’ve come close to winning a couple of times. It just shows that my game is there and it’s just a matter of time,” she said.Closer home, the Women’s Indian Open remains a childhood dream. A win on home soil, she feels, would be special in a way no other victory could match.But Pranavi is already looking beyond those targets. Asked what the next ‘first’ she wants to chase is, she said, “To win an Olympic medal or a Major!”For someone who has already broken barriers at the domestic level and the Asian Games, the ambition is clear: the next frontier is no longer India, but the global arenas of the sport.
Article Summary: Pranavi Urs is the first Indian woman to win an individual gold at the Asian Games. She was so locked into the moment that she did not even realise her final putt was for gold. Her next first could come on the Ladies European Tour where she has been knocking on the door of a maiden victory.

Article Title: Nic Maddinson creates unwanted record for longest duck by a Test opener in 21st century
Article Text:
Australia's Nic Maddinson is bowled on day one of the first cricket test match between South Africa and Australia. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nic Maddinson’s return to Test cricket after nearly a decade got off to a disastrous start as the Australia opener endured a 33-ball duck against South Africa in the first Test at Kingsmead, Durban, on Friday.Maddinson’s 0 off 33 balls is the third-longest duck by an opener in Test history. It is also the longest innings for a duck by a Test opener in the 21st century, making it an unwanted milestone on his comeback to the national side.The 34-year-old was dismissed after Travis Head fell for nine, leaving Australia in early trouble after captain Pat Cummins won the toss and elected to bat on the opening day.Maddinson was drafted into the squad as a replacement for the injured Cameron Green, making a return to the Test set-up after overcoming testicular cancer. His previous Test appearance came during the 2016-17 home summer, when he managed just 27 runs across three matches.However, his recall had come under scrutiny even before the series began, with former Australia opener Matthew Hayden questioning the selectors’ decision to bring back a batter who had not played first-class cricket since early 2025.Speaking on the All Over Bar The Cricket podcast, Hayden launched a scathing attack on the selection panel and questioned the standard of players being picked for the national team.“Where we are at is that we are promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we’ve seen in a generation of cricket,” Hayden said.He also questioned the expectation that players with modest first-class averages could translate that form into success at the highest level, taking aim at chief selector George Bailey and Tony Dodemaide.“And if we continue to lay that out and expect that a bloke averaging 35 is going to average 55 in Test match cricket, George Bailey and Tony Dodemaide, you are dreaming. I will just put it that simply. You are frigging dreaming. And you are piling up this dog s*** explanation, and you are, in my opinion, disrespecting first-class cricket. Absolutely dead set you are. You should be picking guys that are averaging 45 or more, and you can’t, because they don’t want to play,” Hayden said.Maddinson’s first-class average of 37.11 had further fuelled the debate around his selection. Cummins, however, had backed the batter ahead of the series, saying he was settled in his game.With Head also dismissed cheaply, Australia faced an early test of their batting depth against a South African side that recalled Anrich Nortje and opted for two spinners. Kagiso Rabada was left out as he continues his recovery from a hamstring injury.
Article Summary: Maddinson's 0 off 33 balls is the third-longest duck by an opener in Test history. It is also the longest innings for a duck by a Test opener in the 21st century. The 34-year-old was dismissed after Travis Head fell for nine, leaving Australia in early trouble.

Article Title: 'An absolute fluke': How a cameraman's chance zoom exposed Australia's 2018 Sandpapergate scandal
Article Text:
AB de Villiers of South Africa during day 3 of the 3rd Test match between South Africa and Australia at PPC Newlands on March 24, 2018 in Cape Town, South Africa. (File photo)

How an 'absolute fluke' exposed Sandpapergate

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Australia and South Africa began their three-Test series in Durban on Friday, renewing a rivalry that has been marked by the Sandpapergate scandal of 2018. The two teams currently occupy the top two spots in the World Test Championship (WTC) standings, with South Africa entering the series as defending champions after beating Australia in the previous cycle's final.Their first Test in South Africa since the 2018 tour comes with only one player from that controversial Australian trio of Warner, Bancroft, and Smith still in the team: Steve Smith. The scandal saw Smith, then captain, along with David Warner and Cameron Bancroft found guilty of ball-tampering. Smith lost the captaincy and was banned from international and domestic cricket for 12 months. Warner received the same ban and was barred from holding any leadership role in Australian cricket, while Bancroft was banned for nine months. Warner has since retired, and Bancroft is no longer part of Australia's plans.As the teams begin the series opener at Kingsmead, Alvin Naicker, who was overseeing the live broadcast of the infamous Cape Town Test in March 2018, has recalled how a series of chance events led to the scandal being exposed."The way the Australians were caught was an absolute fluke," Alvin Naicker, who was in charge of SuperSport's live broadcast from Newlands, told BBC Sport.The plan had been hatched by Australia's "leadership group" during the lunch break that Saturday. An alert camera operator stayed focused on Bancroft when others might have moved elsewhere, while the person controlling the stadium's big screen showed footage that was also being broadcast to millions of viewers around the world."Coverage of rugby and football is very coordinated. It's camera one and two, then when the ball is dead you tell the story with close-up shots," explains Naicker, as quoted by BBC."Because cricket has so much dead time, there is a lot more storytelling. There are between 80 and 100 people coming together and putting the story together in a matter of seconds, coordinated by the director."Naicker said the 2018 series had begun on a tense note, but the local broadcasters were not specifically looking for signs of cheating by the Australians, despite the incidents during the first two Tests."No one mentioned anything to me," says Naicker.He recalled how the camera operator happened to remain focused on Bancroft as the Australian batter handled the ball."The ball went to the wicketkeeper, then to Bancroft and he was shining the ball," says Naicker. "First it was on his pants, then the next ball, the cameraman happened to stay on Bancroft because he was not shining the ball on his pants, but he was rubbing the ball on his palm.""When he threw the ball on, he put his hand in his pocket. The cameraman - and these are big, big lens cameras - he zoomed into his pocket. The slow-mo operator looked at it, spooled it back and forth, then zoomed in and could see the yellow spot."Bancroft was caught hiding sandpaper in his trousers. Naicker and his team then replayed the footage on the stadium's big screen."When Bancroft looked up at the screen and saw it, he removed it and put it in his jocks," says Naicker. "The cameraman recorded it. It still wasn't live, we played a replay."The footage brought the ball-tampering scandal into the open. In the aftermath, Smith broke down in tears during a live television interview and accepted responsibility. However, he was still handed a 12-month ban from international and domestic cricket and removed as captain.Warner was also banned for 12 months and barred from holding any leadership role in Australian cricket. Bancroft received a nine-month ban from international and domestic cricket.
Article Summary: Australia and South Africa begin their three-Test series in Durban on Friday. The two teams currently occupy the top two spots in the World Test Championship standings. Alvin Naicker, who was overseeing the live broadcast of the infamous Cape Town Test in March 2018, has recalled how a series of chance events led to the scandal.

Article Title: ‘We’re not trying to be any other league’: SA20 COO Lynn Naudé on the league’s rapid rise
Article Text:
Lynn Naudé (left), COO of SA20 (Special Arrangement)

Excerpts

SA20 has grown rapidly in four seasons. What has been the biggest lesson behind that success?

How do you keep SA20 distinct in an increasingly crowded global T20 calendar?

What role has the league played in strengthening South African cricket beyond the professional level?

With overseas leagues expanding, how do you ensure SA20 continues attracting elite international players?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Looking ahead to Season 5, what is the one area where you want fans to notice a clear step forward?

NEW DELHI: Four seasons into its existence, SA20 has already established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. But for COO Lynn Naudé, the league’s rapid rise has been less about chasing quick wins and more about getting the fundamentals right. From securing a prime South African summer window and putting Proteas at the heart of the competition to creating a strong match-day atmosphere, Naudé explains how SA20 has built its identity and what lies ahead in Season 5.I think probably the biggest lesson is that strong foundations matter more than quick wins. From the very start, we were very single-minded about what we believed success looked like. The fan experience, the quality of cricket and putting South African players at the heart of the competition were all important to us. We wanted to make sure SA20 felt like it belonged to South African fans as a starting point, and then we could take it global from there.I think that's probably been one of my biggest learnings. If you can get your basics right, the rest will follow from thereT20 cricket has got a unique feeling to it, and that's possibly a common thread. But I think there are a couple of things that have helped us.First, our window and our ability to secure it in the heart of the South African summer, with great conditions and full stadiums, was a real coup for us.That time of year lends itself to delivering a product that speaks very much to the fans, but also provides a fantastic experience both on broadcast and in the stadium.The second is the quality of the competition. The commitment from Cricket South Africa to make all of its Proteas available to play in the tournament season after season, and to see them compete with the best in the world, means that we have intentionally put cricket at the heart of the product.The third is probably the atmosphere at the venues. I think that's become something quite synonymous with SA20.If I had to wrap it up, I'd say we're not trying to be any other league. We're just trying to be the best version of SA20 that we can be.”It has actually been on multiple levels. The intention was for SA20 to almost become a bastion for South African cricket. There was obviously work that needed to be done to strengthen the talent pipeline.But outside of that, if I look back again on the last five seasons, it's also about the quality of the broadcast, what's improved in terms of the fan experience within the South African sporting context, our venues, the ways of working and how they operate on a day-to-day basis.There's also been a lot of knowledge transfer from SA20 into the greater cricket ecosystem, with some of the standards and expectations that we have for the type of product we want to deliver.We've had the opportunity to expose a lot of young talent in the sporting industry to our ways of working and the culture at SA20.In the lead-up to the 2027 World Cup, what we've tried to do is make sure that the cricket ecosystem, and those who deliver not only on the field but also off it, is better off the back of SA20 and the experience it has brought to the South African cricket landscape.At the highest level, elite players want to play where the cricket is competitive, the conditions are good and the environment is professional. I think that's something we strive to offer, and I think we do offer all three.Our franchises bring global experience and know how to run teams. The players know that when they come here, they'll be tested against strong domestic talent and they'll be playing in front of full stadiums.It's always surprising to me, anecdotally, when I hear players talk about how important it is to them to play in front of a crowd and how different it feels. I guess when you're talented like that, you feel appreciated when you're playing in front of a lot of people.That, coupled with the strong and stable franchise ownership groups that we've got, who invest in those players, offers them opportunities.If you have the opportunity to play in the SA20, you also have the opportunity to play in many other places around the world. I think consistency across all of those things will make sure that we remain attractive to players.Every season we run a fan survey, and it directly shapes what we deliver. Our fans have told us what they want to see more of, and they've also told us what they don't want us to change. Those are the types of things that shape our decisions.Our brand positioning at SA20 is ‘for everyone’, and we take that pretty seriously. On the field, it means competitive, world-class cricket for the dedicated cricket fan. Off the field, it really means a great social occasion for people to come and enjoy the atmosphere, the music and a day out with friends and family.If I have to say what I want fans to take away, it's that we do hear you, we do listen to what you want, and we will always strive to deliver based on the feedback that fans are giving us.
Article Summary: Lynn Naudé, COO of SA20, talks to TOI about the league's rapid rise. SA20 has established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. COO says league's success has been down to getting the fundamentals right. He talks about securing a prime South African summer window.

Article Title: 'India pressed the panic button way too early': Former pacer questions strategy after West Indies defeat
Article Text:
Ranchi: West Indies' captain Shai Hope, right, celebrates with Romario Shepherd after winning the second T20I cricket match of a series between India and West Indies, in Ranchi, Jharkhand. (PTI Photo/Salman Ali)

Aaron questions India's bowling strategy

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Hope and Rutherford lead historic chase

Former India fast bowler Varun Aaron has criticised India's bowling approach after the West Indies pulled off a record chase in the second T20I in Ranchi. Despite India scoring a massive 249/5, the visitors chased down the target of 250, reaching 252/4 in 19.2 overs to level the five-match series 1-1.Aaron believes India’s bowlers moved away from disciplined bowling lengths too early, allowing Shai Hope and Sherfane Rutherford to take control of the match with aggressive batting.India had made a strong start, with Mayank Yadav taking two wickets in the opening over and finishing with three. However, Aaron felt the bowlers failed to build on that advantage by repeatedly switching to yorkers, slower balls and bouncers instead of sticking to consistent lengths."The way Shai Hope and Rutherford played was brilliant. It was almost a Batman-and-Robin kind of partnership: Shai Hope held guard, kept things steady at one end, and Rutherford just kept going. They batted brilliantly, but the Indian bowlers, after that first four or five overs, just completely forgot about bowling length. I think they pressed the panic button way too early,” Aaron told JioStar.He also pointed out that India's attempts to bowl yorkers gave the West Indies opportunities to score boundaries, particularly when Rovman Powell was struggling early in his innings.“They went to their yorkers, slower balls, bouncers, wide bouncers and wide slower balls way too early. Mayank Yadav got three wickets. Two of those three wickets were off proper length. That's exactly what Arshdeep should have done, especially when Rovman Powell was batting at the start and was looking very shaky.“They gave him a few full tosses, trying to bowl yorkers. He got a few boundaries off them, and then they kept building the innings. Since they had those two early wickets from Mayank Yadav, India could have stuck to their lengths a little longer,” he added.The West Indies were struggling at 58/3 before Hope and Rutherford turned the game around with a 120-run partnership. Hope remained unbeaten on 102 off 45 balls, while Rutherford smashed 84 off just 37 deliveries.Their partnership helped the visitors complete the highest successful T20I run chase against India. Earlier, Sanju Samson had scored 82 off 41 balls and Tilak Varma contributed 44 as India posted 249/5, but their efforts ultimately proved insufficient.
Article Summary: Former India fast bowler Varun Aaron has criticised India's bowling approach after the West Indies pulled off a record chase in the second T20I in Ranchi. The visitors chased down the target of 250, reaching 252/4 in 19.2 overs to level the five-match series 1-1.

NEW DELHI: Mayank Yadav's fiery opening spell was one of the positives for India in their second T20I against the West Indies in Ranchi on Friday. The fast bowler regularly clocked speeds above 140 kmph and took two wickets off successive deliveries in the first over, dismissing Kamil Pooran and Shimron Hetmyer. He later bowled Rovman Powell with a delivery clocked at 149 kmph.Mayank finished with three wickets in three overs but conceded 36 runs at an economy rate of 12.00.Despite his early strikes, India failed to defend 249 as the West Indies chased down the target to win by six wickets.India head coach Gautam Gambhir said the match could not be judged by what happened in the opening over."I have played enough cricket to know that games are not decided in the first over. A game of cricket is won or lost by the way you play consistently over the course of 40 overs," Gambhir said at the post match conference.Gambhir also backed Mayank to continue bowling at his natural pace instead of holding back."A fast bowler should bowl like a fast bowler.He is not a slower bowler," he said."If you can bowl at 150 kmph, bowl at 150. If you can bowl at 120, bowl at 120. When you are playing as a fast bowler, it is your duty to bowl fast, like a fast bowler," he added."That is what he did today, and that is why he was successful," Gambhir said.Gambhir also spoke about the need for a better contest between bat and ball after another high-scoring match. He had earlier described the Guwahati pitch as a featherbed.Asked whether India wanted better pitches, Gambhir said he wanted conditions that gave both batters and bowlers a fair chance."Don't you want a good competition between the bat and the ball? New Zealand fast bowler Will O'Rourke will miss the upcoming home series against India as he continues recovering from injuries to his left hamstring and calf.The 25-year-old has been ruled out as a precaution, with New Zealand keen to ensure he is fully fit for their important four-Test tour of Australia in December.New Zealand will face India in five T20Is, five ODIs and two Tests, beginning with the first T20I in Christchurch on October 22.O'Rourke had only recently returned to international cricket after spending seven months out with a back stress fracture. However, he injured his hamstring on the final day of New Zealand's third Test against England before suffering a calf strain during training in late August.New Zealand coach Rob Walter said the decision was made after discussions with O'Rourke and the team's medical staff."It's obviously disappointing for Will to have to miss such a marquee tour at home against India," said Walter."He was set to feature in both the ODI and Test series, but following subsequent discussions, we all agreed it was best for him to take some more time to rehabilitate both injuries and safely build up his bowling loads."New Zealand had also announced on Friday that Mark Chapman and Zak Foulkes would miss the T20I series because of injuries.New Zealand are taking a cautious approach with O'Rourke because their fast bowlers will be important during a busy period of international cricket."Our pace bowling resources will be critical over the next few months so we're taking a conservative approach to Will's return to ensure he's fully fit before he takes the field again," Walter said.The team hopes O'Rourke will return to action for Canterbury in the Plunket Shield, New Zealand's first-class domestic competition, in late December. If his recovery goes as planned, he could be available for the opening Test against Australia in Perth on December 9."Ideally he'll be able to return for Canterbury in the Plunket Shield in late December, and in a perfect world he'll be ready to go for the opening Test against Australia in Perth on December 9," he added.
Article Summary: New Zealand fast bowler Will O'Rourke will miss the upcoming home series against India. The 25-year-old is recovering from injuries to his left hamstring and calf. New Zealand will face India in five T20Is, five ODIs and two Tests, beginning with the first T20I in Christchurch on October 22.

The conditions were in our favour with the ball, and we found the right length. There were plenty of short and back-of-the-length deliveries, which worked well for us,” Johnson said.After opting to bat, Australia ‘A’ made a brisk start, with Mitchell Owen launching Arshad Khan (3-56) for two sixes to plunder 17 runs in the opening over. Owen’s promising cameo ended at 25, but Josh Philippe (58) and Sam Konstas (67), who registered his maiden List A half-century, stitched together a 101-run stand for the second wicket.SCORES: Australia ‘A’ 275 in 49.5 overs (S Konstas 67, J Philippe 58; A Khan 3-56, Y Thakur 2-46) beat India ‘A’ 206 in 45.2 overs (R Patidar 67; S Johnson 3-35, R Meredith 2-31, T Sangha 2-42) by 69 runs.

Article Title: Shreyas Iyer captains the way he wants: Lockie Ferguson
Article Text:
Shreyas Iyer (AFP Photo)

MUMBAI: Shreyas Iyer ’s appointment as India’s T20I captain after the team’s World Cup triumph earlier this year surprised many. India will soon travel to New Zealand for a one-and-a-half-month all-format tour, starting with a five-match T20I series in Christchurch on Oct 22. Waiting there will be Iyer’s Punjab Kings teammate and New Zealand pacer Lockie Ferguson, who has only praise for his leadership.“The best captains I’ve played under have been really consistent and don’t ride the ups and downs of the game, particularly in T20 cricket where it ebbs and flows so quickly,” Ferguson said during an interaction organised by Sony Sports. “Shreyas is calm, speaks clearly, has a clear plan and gives you feedback, but also allows you to bowl to your plan because he knows that’s your strength. Those are the guys you want by your side because, regardless of the outcome, they thank you and give you every opportunity to succeed. ”Ferguson said Iyer had handled the pressure of leading India well. “He’s a level-headed character. It can be difficult with the external pressures that come with playing for India, but he seems to have found a clear way to interact with fans while staying humble and consistent with his process,” Ferguson said.“He plays the game the way he wants to and captains the way he wants to. I’m not surprised he’s India’s captain, and I really enjoyed my time with him at Punjab. ”Ferguson is also impressed with India’s current batting depth. Abhishek Sharma, Ishan Kishan, Sanju Samson, Tilak Varma and Iyer have helped India move on after Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma retired from the format following the 2024 T20 World Cup.“The whole country wants to play for India, and that drives competition for places and pushes the game forward. The IPL has played a major role in that,” Ferguson said. “What I’ve noticed most in recent years is the lack of fear among players, which probably comes from the intense competition for spots.”Ferguson also spoke highly of Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, who has generated buzz since being included in India’s T20I squad. “He’s a high-quality player. We had some games against him in the IPL and, clearly, he’s an amazing talent,” he said. “It’s an exciting opportunity for him to travel, experience New Zealand and see how cricket is played here. The conditions are different, so there will be challenges, but it’s going to be exciting. ”

Article Title: IND vs WI 2nd T20I: Shai Hope, Sherfane Rutherford power West Indies to record chase against India
Article Text:

RANCHI: West Indies skipper Shai Hope struck his second T20 International hundred to power the visitors to a stunning six-wicket win over India in the second game of the series here on Friday.Chasing 250 after India posted 249/5, West Indies reached 252/4 with nine balls to spare — their highest successful chase in T20Is and the second-highest in the format, behind South Africa’s 259/4 against West Indies in Centurion in 2023.The chase began in the worst possible fashion for the visitors. Mayank Yadav (3/36) struck twice in the opening over to leave the West Indies reeling, but Hope refused to allow the early setback to dictate the course of the innings.Rovman Powell joined his captain and the pair began the repair work, putting on 53 for the third wicket. Once Powell departed, Sherfane Rutherford walked in with a clear intent to attack and the game began to swing decisively towards the visitors.Rutherford and Hope produced the partnership that broke India’s grip on the contest, adding 120 off just 54 balls for the fourth wicket. Rutherford was the aggressor, taking the attack apart with seven fours and seven sixes in his 84 off 37 balls.Hope remained the constant presence at the other end, combining clean hitting with calculated strokeplay.By the time Rutherford departed, West Indies still needed 72 off 35 balls. Romario Shepherd then provided the final burst, smashing an unbeaten 34 off 13 balls, including three fours and three sixes, as West Indies completed the chase with nine balls to spare.For Hope, the hundred continued an extraordinary tour. The West Indies captain had already struck two centuries during the ODI series before making a half-century in a losing cause in the opening T20I.Earlier, India had appeared to have put themselves firmly in command, largely through Sanju Samson’s timely return to form. Under pressure after four subdued outings and with the growing conversation around teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi waiting in the wings, Samson responded with an assured 82 off 41 balls.Rather than relying entirely on the big hits for which he is often known, the Kerala wicketkeeper-batter repeatedly found gaps with crisp drives and deft touches before choosing his moments to clear the boundary.Samson struck nine fours and four sixes, and West Indies were left to rue two dropped chances. He and hometown favourite Ishan Kishan added 97 off just 43 balls for the second wicket, with Kishan contributing a lively 43 off 22 as the Ranchi crowd embraced its local hero. Roston Chase briefly slowed India’s charge, claiming the first three wickets.

Chasing 250 after India posted 249/5, West Indies reached 252/4 with nine balls to spare. It was their highest successful chase in T20Is and the second-highest in the format, behind South Africa’s 259/4 against West Indies in Centurion in 2023.

Article Title: Only second player ever! Shai Hope scripts history against India with record-breaking ton

Hope joins elite T20I list

West Indies captain Shai Hope created history on Friday by becoming only the second player in the world to score centuries in all three formats of international cricket against India.He achieved the milestone with an unbeaten 102 off 45 balls in the second T20I in Ranchi, helping the West Indies chase down a target of 250 and win by six wickets.Hope's explosive innings guided his team to victory in just 18.3 overs, with four wickets down.The result also marked the highest successful T20I run chase in West Indies history and the highest successful chase by any team against India in the format.Former Australia all-rounder Shane Watson is the only other player to have scored at least one century in Tests, ODIs and T20Is against India. Watson achieved the feat during his international career, scoring one hundred in each format.Before his latest knock, Hope had already scored one Test century and five ODI centuries against India. His unbeaten hundred in Ranchi completed the set by giving him his first T20I century against the Indian team.England's Jos Buttler and Australia's Glenn Maxwell have also scored centuries against India in Tests and T20Is, but neither has scored a hundred against India in ODIs.Hope is the second West Indies batter, after Evin Lewis , to score a T20I century against India. Lewis has scored two hundreds against India in the shortest format, making him one of the few players to achieve the feat more than once.Hope's latest achievement adds to his growing record against India and highlights his ability to perform across formats. His match-winning innings in Ranchi not only secured a historic personal milestone but also helped West Indies level the five-match T20I series at 1-1.
Article Summary: Shai Hope becomes only the second player in the world to score centuries in all three formats of international cricket against India. Article Title: 'You cannot put a number': Captain Shreyas Iyer blames heavy dew after India's defeat to West Indies

India captain Shreyas Iyer said heavy dew and a batter-friendly pitch made it difficult for his team to defend a massive total of 249 against West Indies in the second T20I. Article Title: 'Gambhir is chopping and changing all the time': Ex-Australia player calls India 'unsettled', explains why

Former Australian all-rounder Shane Watson has criticised India head coach Gautam Gambhir, saying frequent changes to the playing XI and batting order have affected the team's consistency across formats.Since becoming head coach in mid-2024, Gambhir has guided India to Champions Trophy and T20 World Cup titles. However, the team has struggled in other competitions, suffering home Test series defeats against New Zealand and South Africa, along with losses in ODI and T20I cricket.“The thing that you continue to see and the reason India have been inconsistent under Gambhir is the chopping and changing around the batting order all the time. Article Title: First time in 149 years: Australia make unique record in first Test vs South Africa
Article Text:
Australia's Steven Smith takes evasive action against a raising ball on day one of the first cricket test match between South Africa and Australia, in Durban, South Africa, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (AP Photo)

Australia fielded the oldest playing XI in their men's Test history in the first Test against South Africa in Durban on Friday, with all 11 players aged 30 or above. It was the first time in 149 years that an Australian men's Test XI did not include a player in his 20s.Captain Pat Cummins won the toss and chose to bat, with Australia's playing XI having an average age of 34.59. According to cricket statistician Ric Finlay, as quoted by News18, it was the seventh-oldest Test XI of all time and the oldest in around 100 years.At 38, spinner Nathan Lyon was the oldest member of the side, while Matt Renshaw, 30, was the youngest. Five players were aged 35 or above: Lyon, Steve Smith (37), Mitchell Starc (36), Alex Carey (35) and Josh Hazlewood (35).Australia's regular rotation of openers had ensured that the team included at least one player under 30 for months. However, that changed with the recall of Nic Maddinson, 34, for the Durban Test.Maddinson was playing his first Test since December 2016. He has featured in only three Tests, all of them in that year.Australia's 18-member squad has an average age of around 32.6, with only three players under 30. Cooper Connolly, 23, is the youngest, followed by Cameron Green, 27, and Sam Harper, 29.Green has regularly featured in the playing XI but has struggled for form in recent times.Meanwhile, South Africa's pace attack, without their spearhead Kagiso Rabada, restricted Australia to 187/6 before bad light and rain brought an early end to the first day of the opening Test at Kingsmead in Durban on Friday.Despite Rabada's absence, Anrich Nortje, Wiaan Mulder and Marco Jansen made good use of the early movement and bounce on a pitch with a tinge of grass after Australia chose to bat. Mulder struck first by dismissing Travis Head for nine, before Jansen ended Maddinson's scoreless 33-ball stay on his return to Test cricket, leaving Australia at 24/2.Marnus Labuschagne, who scored 37, and Smith, who made 25, steadied the innings with a 60-run partnership for the third wicket off 94 balls. Smith, who moved past Steve Waugh to become Australia's third-highest run-scorer in men's Tests, hit two sixes off spinner Keshav Maharaj before Jansen dismissed him after lunch.Australia had won the toss and opted to bat in the first match of the three-Test World Test Championship series.

Article Title: ‘Olympic gold jeetna hai’: Kumkum Mohod’s big dream after ending Korea’s stranglehold in archery at Asian Games 2026
Article Text:
Kumkum Mohod

TimesofIndia.com

Kumkum Mohod

Manifestation: ‘I had been visualising this for a year’

Kumkum Mohod (AP Photo)

Road to the final: Learning from the best, then beating her

‘My family always supported me’

Gold medallist India's Kumkum Anil Mohod, Ankita Bhakat and Kirti celebrate on the podium during the victory ceremony. (Reuters Photo)

Beyond archery: Drawing, crafts and a dream before sleep

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The ultimate dream: Olympic gold

(Credit: Special arrangement)

NEW DELHI: For years, Kumkum Mohod had watched South Korean archers closely, studying their technique and trying to understand what made them so dominant in recurve archery. She observed their movements, learnt from their approach and looked at the qualities that had made them role models for young Indian archers like her.But when the 17-year-old stood on the shooting line at the Asian Games , just seconds away from releasing her arrow, she had a message for herself: the Koreans were not unbeatable.“Maine match shuru hone se khud ko bol diya tha, woh 10 maarte hain, to mujhe bhi 10 hi maarna hai [I told myself before the match began: they shoot 10s too, so I have to shoot 10s as well],” Asian Games 2026 gold medallist archer Kumkum Mohod toldin an exclusive interview.The 17-year-old made history by winning the women’s individual recurve gold at the Asian Games, beating the Republic of Korea’s Oh Yejin in the final.In doing so, she ended South Korea’s hold on the individual recurve gold at the Games and helped India secure a quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.Before leaving for Aichi-Nagoya, Kumkum had already imagined herself standing on the top of the podium.She had also visualised beating her inspiration, South Korea’s Kang Chaeyoung, whom she eventually defeated in the quarterfinals on her way to the historic gold.Kumkum became the first Indian to win an individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. She also won gold in the women’s recurve team event and silver in the mixed team event with Dhiraj Bommadevara, finishing the Games with three medals.“Until now, no one had managed to do it. But we Indians have done it. We have put the Koreans on a pedestal, as if they are the only ones who can do it and hit those scores. Before the match began, I told myself that they shoot 10s too, and we have to shoot 10s as well,” she said.For Kumkum, the feeling of becoming an Asian Games champion is still sinking in. The young archer said the result did not come as a complete surprise because she had been visualising the moment for a year, even before she stepped onto the field in Japan.For a year leading up to the Asian Games, she repeated the same words five times before going to sleep: “Kumkum, Asian Games gold jeetna hai” (Kumkum, you have to win Asian Games gold). She would then say “Hare Krishna”, reflecting her devotion to Lord Krishna.Her belief was tested against some of the world's best archers. Kumkum defeated South Korea’s reigning world champion and Olympic medallist Kang Chaeyoung 6-3 in the quarterfinals before beating China’s Zhu Jingyi 6-2 in the semifinals.In the final, she held her nerve against South Korea’s Oh Yejin. The contest ended 5-5 after five sets, forcing a shoot-off. Oh shot an eight, while Kumkum hit a 10 to seal the gold medal.Kumkum had been trailing during the match and needed to win the fifth set to stay in contention. She responded by shooting a perfect 30 to force the shoot-off before producing the decisive 10.“The final went really well. I was trailing, but I remained strong. I believed in myself and knew I could do it because I had been visualising this for the past year. I kept imagining that I would face Kang in a match and that it would be a final,” Kumkum said.When Oh shot an eight in the shoot-off, Kumkum had to focus on her own shot rather than the possibility of winning. She knew she had to deliver, regardless of what her opponent had scored.“I had made up my mind that day that I had to prove myself. My first thought was, ‘Kumkum, you still have to shoot a good shot.’ Even if she had shot a 10, I was very confident at that moment,” she said.“I enjoyed that moment while shooting. There is always some pressure, but I tried to reduce it. Anyone who says there is no pressure is absolutely wrong. Sport is about nerves and thrilling moments. There is always adrenaline, and you have to overcome it. The person who manages to do that wins,” she said.Kumkum's journey to the gold medal included victories over some of the world's leading archers. But one of the most memorable moments for her was beating Kang, an archer she had admired and learnt from since the beginning of her career.Kang had been Kumkum's inspiration because of her technique, focus, composure and ability to deliver under pressure. Kumkum paid particular attention to her release and follow-through, as well as the way she maintained her technique in crucial moments.At the Asian Games, however, the young Indian found herself competing against the very archer she had looked up to for years - and came out on top.“Kang’s shooting technique is very good. Her release is excellent, and she does not drop her bow after the follow-through. Her shooting is very strong,” Kumkum said.So, the victory carried special meaning. After the match, Kumkum exchanged a high-five with her opponent and told her, “Good shooting, good shooting.”Kang smiled and congratulated her.“I have learnt a lot from her, and I was happy. She is a legend of the sport. She has made her country proud by winning medals, and now I have done the same. I am proud that I have made my country proud,” Kumkum said.Behind Kumkum’s success is a family that continued to believe in her, even when her performances were not going as planned.Her father, Anil Mohod, runs a business making sweet boxes. As Kumkum was good at academics, her father initially wanted her to focus on her studies. But when he saw her growing interest in archery, her family supported her sporting ambitions while ensuring that she did not neglect her education.Kumkum is the couple’s only child and is currently in Class 12.“I joined archery, and within six months, I won a medal. After that, I learnt about the Olympics and understood what the sport could lead to. I also learnt that India had not won a medal in this event. My interest grew, and I started working harder,” she said.Her family’s faith in her remained strong even during difficult periods.“When I was not doing well, my family told me that I could do it. They have supported me a lot, and I never faced any problems because of them,” she said.Now, following her historic achievement, the Mohod household has been welcoming a steady stream of visitors. Neighbours, friends, relatives, sports associations and fellow sportspersons have been arriving to congratulate the family.Kumkum said the celebrations have kept everyone busy, with little time to rest.“It feels like a wedding atmosphere at home. People keep coming and going, and we are hardly getting any sleep. All thanks to Krishna ji,” she said.Away from the archery range, Kumkum enjoys spending time with a paintbrush and a colour palette. Drawing and craftwork are among her favourite hobbies, giving her a break from the demands of training and competition.“I like drawing and crafting. I also enjoy making things with my hands,” she said.She also enjoys watching television shows and films. Her favourites include Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah and sports-based films such as Dangal, Mary Kom, Ghoomer and Bhaag Milkha Bhaag.Unlike many teenagers, Kumkum has never had Facebook or Instagram accounts. She also disabled YouTube a few months before the Asian Games. Drawing, craftwork and reading are among the activities she enjoys away from the range.“I never had Facebook or Instagram. I also disabled YouTube a few months before the Asian Games. My crafts, drawing and reading books help me a lot,” she said.Kumkum has already achieved a major milestone by winning three medals at the Asian Games and helping India secure a quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. But she has a bigger dream — winning India's first Olympic gold medal in archery.The words she repeated before going to sleep for a year - “Kumkum, Asian Games gold jeetna hai” - now reflect a new ambition: “Kumkum, Olympic gold jeetna hai.”At home, a small message on the wall serves as a reminder of what she wants to achieve.“LA 2028 gold is the target. That is the dream. I do not want to think too far ahead just yet, but that is the target. I will work hard for it and strengthen myself mentally,” Kumkum signed off.
Article Summary: Kumkum Mohod is the first Indian to win an individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. The 17-year-old made history by beating the Republic of Korea’s Oh Yejin in the final. She also won gold in the women's recurvies team event and silver in the mixed team event.

Article Title: Historic Olympic quota, multiple medals — but no salary: India’s compound archery coach unhappy over payment delay
Article Text:
Sahil Jadhav, left, and Chikitha Taniparthi, right, celebrate with coach Dave Cousins after winning the compound mixed team archery gold. (PTI Photo)

A historic breakthrough, but a salary dispute

Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthi with team coach Dave Cousins during the Asian Games. (PTI Photo)

AAI, SAI say payment will be cleared soon

Building towards LA 2028

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India's compound archers made history at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games by becoming the first nation to secure an Olympic quota in the discipline. But while the team celebrated a landmark achievement and a rich medal haul, the foreign coach who helped guide them to success was left unhappy over a salary delay stretching beyond three months.American Dave Cousins, appointed as India's chief compound archery coach in May, is learnt to have threatened to quit and leave the country if his pending dues were not cleared, as per a PTI report.The development has raised questions about the support extended to a coach who has already delivered significant results as India builds towards the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. However, the Archery Association of India (AAI) and the Sports Authority of India (SAI) have acknowledged the delay, attributing it to a technical issue and saying the matter has now been resolved, with the payment expected to be cleared shortly."He has spoken to some officials and said if the dues are not cleared he's leaving home. He's really unhappy with the way he's been treated for three months... he's not been paid so far," sources told PTI.Cousins helped India win three gold medals and a bronze in compound archery at the Asian Games, contributing to the country's overall haul of five gold, two silver and two bronze across recurve and compound events.The biggest breakthrough came in the mixed-team event, where the relatively unfancied Indian pair of Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthi stunned South Korea in a shoot-off after the final was tied 157-157 over four ends.The victory secured India its first-ever Olympic quota in compound archery, a discipline that will feature a mixed-team event at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.Cousins had taken charge of India's compound programme with the responsibility of building a competitive unit for the Olympics. His results at the Asian Games came with a group that had faced questions about its ability to deliver at the highest level.The American had also guided 18-year-old Prithika Pradeep to her maiden World Cup bronze at the Madrid stage in Spain.Reflecting on India's Asian Games campaign, Cousins had stressed that preparation, rather than medal predictions, was the team's priority."The only thing we were willing to commit to is that our athletes would go prepared and that they would execute the process as best they could," he had said."When the training is right, the preparation is right and the ecosystem is right, these are the results you get. We're exceptionally happy to clinch the first-ever compound archery spot for the Olympic Games. That's a huge thing for us right now."AAI treasurer Dr Joris Paulose Ummacheril acknowledged the delay but said the issue had been resolved and the payment would be made shortly."There was some issue with the Sports Authority of India (SAI), so the payment got delayed. But it has all been worked out, and it will be paid within two days," Joris told PTI.An SAI official in New Delhi also attributed the delay to a technical problem involving the bank, adding that the matter was being processed."We have already spoken to him and assured him that the payment is under process. It got delayed because of a technical issue with the bank, and it should be done within a couple of days," the official said.The assurances suggest that the dispute could be resolved soon, although the episode has highlighted the administrative challenges that can undermine the momentum generated by sporting success.Cousins, 49, is a former world No. 1 who won World Archery Championship titles in 1999 and 2003. His appointment in May followed the departure of Sergio Pagni, under whom India swept all five archery gold medals at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou.Meanwhile, the federation is also in talks with South Korean coach Park Chae-soon to take charge of India's recurve programme ahead of LA 2028. Park, who coached South Korea's women's team at the London 2012 Olympics and men's team at Rio 2016, is expected to join by December.With India's archers building momentum towards the next Olympics, Cousins' contribution has already produced a landmark result in compound archery. The historic quota and multiple Asian Games medals have strengthened India's prospects in a discipline making its Olympic debut in Los Angeles.
Article Summary: India's compound archers made history at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games by becoming the first nation to secure an Olympic quota in the discipline. Coach Dave Cousins is learnt to have threatened to quit and leave the country if his pending dues were not cleared. The development has raised questions about the support extended to a coach who has already delivered significant results as India builds towards the 2028 Olympics.

Article Title: ‘I was a daughter of Himachal’: Ritu Negi’s heartbreak after home state drops Asian Games gold medallist from Rs 1 crore reward list
Article Text:
Indian women's Kabaddi player Ritu Negi. (ANI Photo)

‘Why is Himachal Pradesh behaving this way at this stage of my career?’

India women's kabaddi team after winning the Asian Games gold medal in Japan.

Her father asks: Does a daughter stop belonging to her state after marriage?

Why three kabaddi players were awarded Rs 1 crore each

Government promises to review the decision

Another gold medal, but a different kind of disappointment
